questions.q: Why do most real organizations end up with more than one data catalog?
options: Because a single catalog can only index 1,000 tables
Each platform they adopt ships its own native catalog scoped to its own objects, and adopting multiple platforms means multiple catalogs by default
Because governance teams deliberately choose to build redundant catalogs
Because regulations require at least two separate catalogs
questions.explain: The lesson frames this as a predictable consequence of adopting multiple platforms, not a planning failure or a rule.

questions.q: In the federation hub pattern, what role does each platform-native catalog continue to play?
options: It is deleted once the hub is built
It becomes read-only and loses its own permission model
It stops receiving any new metadata
It stays the real source of truth for its own platform's permissions and lineage; the hub is a read layer above it
questions.explain: The hub pulls from platform-native catalogs and presents a combined search surface — it doesn't replace them as the source of truth.

questions.q: What is the main tradeoff between pull-based synchronization and API-based federated search?
options: There is no meaningful difference between the two approaches
API-based search requires no network connectivity at all
Pull-based sync is always faster than API-based search in every scenario
Pull-based sync can go stale between scheduled pulls; API-based search avoids staleness but costs latency and depends on every platform's API being available
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly names staleness as the cost of pull-based sync and latency/availability as the cost of live API-based federated search.

questions.q: According to the lesson, where does most of the real effort in a catalog-integration project actually go?
options: Writing marketing copy for the new catalog
Building the search bar's visual design
The translation layer — mapping one platform's tags, owners, and classifications onto another's
Training users on keyboard shortcuts
questions.explain: Permissions and classifications don't transfer automatically between platforms — translating between their concepts is where most integration effort actually goes.

questions.q: How does a federated or data-mesh operating model (Chapter 2) typically show up at the catalog layer?
options: It requires deleting every platform-native catalog immediately
It has no relationship to catalog architecture at all
Platform-native catalogs stay authoritative at the domain level, with a lighter integration layer, like a federation hub, sitting above them
It mandates API-based federated search specifically, with no alternative
questions.explain: The lesson connects the operating-model choice from Chapter 2 directly to which catalog-integration pattern tends to fit: federated/mesh models keep native catalogs authoritative with a hub above them.
